body:
What Is a Computer?

A computer is an electronic device that accepts data and instructions, processes the data according to those instructions, stores information and produces useful output. Computers are used for calculations, maintaining records, preparing documents, communication, education, banking and many other activities.

A computer can perform different tasks because its behaviour is controlled by programs. The same computer may calculate examination results, prepare a letter, display a photograph or play an audio recording when suitable software is available.

Computer: An electronic device that accepts data, processes it according to instructions, stores data and produces information as output.

Data and Information

Data consists of raw facts, figures or observations that have not necessarily been organised into a meaningful result. Information is data that has been processed or arranged so that it is meaningful and useful.

Consider the marks obtained by a student in 3 subjects: 65, 75 and 80. These individual marks are data. When the computer adds them and produces a total of 220, the calculated total is information. The original marks remain data used in the calculation.

The distinction depends partly on purpose. A calculated total can itself become input data for another operation, such as preparing a class result.

Basic Functions of a Computer

A computer performs the following fundamental functions:

  1. Input: Receiving data and instructions through devices such as a keyboard, mouse or scanner.
  2. Processing: Performing operations on the data according to instructions. The Central Processing Unit performs the main general-purpose processing tasks.
  3. Output: Presenting results through devices such as a monitor, printer or speaker.
  4. Storage: Retaining data, instructions and results for immediate or later use.
  5. Control: Coordinating operations so that the different parts of the computer work together correctly.

Input, processing and output describe the central data processing cycle. Storage and control support the cycle. Processing may involve addition, subtraction, comparison, sorting or another operation specified by the software.

Practical Example: Processing an Application

Consider a clerk using a computer in a public office in Gujarat to prepare an acknowledgement for an application. This is an illustrative example of computer use, not a description of a particular government software system.

  1. The clerk enters the applicant's name and application details using a keyboard.
  2. The application software processes the entered information according to its instructions.
  3. The computer displays the acknowledgement on the monitor.
  4. The clerk may print the acknowledgement or save the record on a storage device.

The keyboard provides input, the CPU performs processing, the monitor and printer provide output, and the storage device retains the saved record. The operating system helps the application use these hardware components.

Computers connected to communication networks can also exchange information electronically. Applications such as electronic mail and online public services use this capability, but a computer does not require an internet connection to perform ordinary local calculations or document processing.

Important Characteristics and Limitations

  • Speed: A computer can perform large numbers of operations rapidly.
  • Accuracy: Correct instructions and valid input generally allow highly accurate results. Incorrect data or instructions can produce incorrect output.
  • Storage capacity: Computers can retain large amounts of information for future retrieval.
  • Consistency: A computer can repeat the same defined operation without human fatigue.
  • Versatility: Different programs allow the same computer to perform different types of tasks.

Garbage In, Garbage Out (GIGO): Incorrect or unsuitable input can produce incorrect results even when the computer operates properly. High processing speed does not guarantee that the input data or the instructions are correct.

Prelims focus

  • Data consists of raw facts; information is meaningful processed data.
  • The basic processing cycle consists of input, processing and output.
  • The CPU performs the main general-purpose processing operations.
  • Storage retains data and results for use when required.
  • Trap: A computer does not automatically guarantee correct information when the input or instructions are incorrect.

[Sources: National Institute of Open Schooling, Data Entry Operations, Lesson 1, Basics of Computer, sections 1.3 and 1.3.1; CBSE, Computer Science, Class XI, Unit 1, Chapter 1, Computer Fundamentals; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 122–123; NCERT, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Class 12, Chapter 8, Transport and Communication, printed pp. 78–79. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Computer Fundamentals: Meaning, Functions and the Data Processing Cycle

Meaning of Computer Generations

Computers have developed through major changes in electronic technology, physical size, speed, cost and capabilities. The term generation of computers is used to describe important stages in this development.

Traditional computer textbooks commonly explain 5 generations. The first 4 are identified mainly by changes in electronic components. The fifth is usually associated with the development of artificial intelligence and more advanced forms of computing.

The division is a teaching classification rather than a universally fixed historical timetable. Technologies often overlapped, and different textbooks assign somewhat different starting and ending years.

First Generation: Vacuum Tubes

First-generation electronic computers were developed mainly during the 1940s and 1950s. They used vacuum tubes as essential electronic switching components.

Vacuum tubes controlled the movement of electrons and made electronic calculations possible. However, computers containing large numbers of these tubes occupied considerable space, consumed substantial electricity and produced significant heat.

ENIAC, publicly introduced in 1946, is a well-known example of an early vacuum-tube electronic computer.

Second Generation: Transistors

Second-generation computers appeared mainly from the late 1950s. They used transistors in place of vacuum tubes for many electronic operations.

A transistor is a semiconductor device that can control electrical signals. Compared with vacuum tubes, transistors are much smaller, generally require less power and are more reliable.

The use of transistors helped reduce computer size, electricity consumption and operating costs while improving performance and reliability.

Third Generation: Integrated Circuits

Third-generation computers became prominent from the mid-1960s. Their defining technology was the integrated circuit (IC).

An integrated circuit combines multiple electronic components and their connections on a small semiconductor chip. Instead of assembling large numbers of separate components, manufacturers could place circuits together in a compact form.

Integrated circuits made computers smaller, more reliable and increasingly capable. They also supported improvements in operating systems and interactive computer use.

Fourth Generation: Microprocessors

The fourth generation is associated with the development and widespread use of microprocessors, beginning in the 1970s.

A microprocessor incorporates the functions of a central processing unit onto a single integrated circuit chip. Advances in large-scale integration made it possible to place increasingly complex electronic circuits on small chips.

Microprocessor-based computing contributed significantly to the development and widespread availability of personal computers and, later, many portable computing devices.

Fifth Generation: Artificial Intelligence-Oriented Computing

In conventional textbook classifications, the fifth generation is associated with artificial intelligence (AI), natural-language interaction, learning capabilities and advanced processing techniques.

The objective is to develop systems capable of performing tasks such as recognising speech, interpreting information and assisting with decisions. AI-based applications are already used in many computers and smartphones.

Unlike the earlier generations, the fifth generation does not have one universally accepted replacement component or a universally agreed starting date. AI-based software can run on ordinary microprocessor-based computers. Therefore, AI capability alone does not establish that a machine belongs to a completely separate hardware generation.

Comparison of Computer Generations

GenerationApproximate periodDefining technologyMain development
First1940s to mid-1950sVacuum tubesEarly electronic computers
SecondLate 1950s to mid-1960sTransistorsSmaller and more reliable systems
ThirdMid-1960s to 1970sIntegrated circuitsCompact and increasingly capable systems
FourthFrom the 1970s onwardMicroprocessors and large-scale integrationPersonal and portable computing
FifthAI-oriented research from the late 20th century onwardAI and advanced computing techniquesIntelligent information processing

The periods are approximate and overlap. For objective questions, the most dependable distinction is the technology associated with each generation, rather than treating an approximate year as an absolute boundary.

Understanding the Progression

The sequence from vacuum tubes to transistors, integrated circuits and microprocessors shows how electronic components became smaller and more highly integrated. This enabled manufacturers to produce increasingly compact and capable computers.

Artificial intelligence represents a different emphasis. It concerns what a computer system can accomplish through advanced processing and software rather than the invention of one replacement switching component.

Prelims focus

  • First generation: vacuum tubes.
  • Second generation: transistors.
  • Third generation: integrated circuits.
  • Fourth generation: microprocessors.
  • Fifth generation in conventional textbook classification: artificial intelligence-oriented computing.
  • Trap: A microprocessor belongs to the fourth-generation technological transition; AI does not automatically mean that an entirely new hardware technology has replaced it.

[Sources: CBSE, Computer Science, Class XI, Unit 1, Chapter 1, Computer Fundamentals, section on computer generations; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Open University, Fundamentals of Computers & Information Technology, 2020 edition, Unit 1, section 1.4, printed pp. 3–5; CBSE, Installation Technician: Computing and Peripherals, Class XI, Chapter 2, Computer System Fundamentals, section on generations of computers, printed pp. 25–27. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Generations of Computers: From Vacuum Tubes to Artificial Intelligence

body:
Meaning of Hardware

Computer hardware refers to the physical components of a computer system. These are the parts that can be physically observed or handled, such as the keyboard, monitor, motherboard, memory modules, storage drives and processor.

Hardware performs physical operations, including receiving signals, processing data, retaining information and displaying results. Hardware works with software, which supplies the instructions necessary to perform useful tasks.

Hardware: The physical electronic, electrical and mechanical components of a computer system.

Major Categories of Computer Hardware

Computer hardware can be grouped according to the function it performs.

FunctionHardware examplesPurpose
InputKeyboard, mouse, scannerSupplies data and instructions
ProcessingCPUExecutes instructions and processes data
Working memoryRAMHolds information needed during current operations
StorageHDD, SSD, USB flash driveRetains files and information
OutputMonitor, printer, speakerPresents results
InterconnectionMotherboard, portsConnects components and allows communication

The System Unit

In a conventional desktop computer, the system unit is the main enclosure containing important internal components. It commonly includes the motherboard, CPU, RAM, storage drives and power supply.

The exact arrangement varies. A laptop may combine the keyboard, display and internal components into one portable device. An all-in-one computer may place major internal components behind its screen.

Motherboard

The motherboard is the main circuit board connecting important computer components. It provides connections through which the CPU, memory, storage devices and other hardware communicate.

The motherboard is not the same as the CPU. The CPU executes instructions, while the motherboard provides the physical connections that allow components to work together.

Central Processing Unit

The CPU is the primary general-purpose processor. It carries out instructions and performs calculations, comparisons and control operations.

The CPU is normally a component installed on or connected to the main circuit board. It should not be confused with the complete system unit or the entire computer.

Memory and Storage

RAM holds instructions and data needed during active operations. A storage device such as an SSD or HDD retains saved documents, installed applications and other files when the computer is switched off.

Power Supply

The power supply provides electrical power in a form suitable for the computer's components. It does not perform the main data processing operations.

Internal and External Hardware

Internal hardware is located inside the computer enclosure. Examples include the CPU, RAM and an internal storage drive.

External hardware includes devices connected outside the enclosure, such as an external keyboard, printer, external storage drive or monitor.

A peripheral device is a device used with a computer to provide input, output, storage or another supporting function. Peripherals may be externally attached or built into a device.

The distinction between internal and external does not determine the device's function. For example, an internal storage drive and an external storage drive can both retain saved files.

Ports and Connections

A port provides a connection through which a device can exchange information with a computer or receive a supported service such as power.

A USB port may connect a keyboard, mouse or flash drive. A display connection may carry video output to a monitor. The function depends on the port and the connected device.

CPU, system unit and computer are different terms. The CPU performs processing. The system unit houses several components. The complete computer system includes the components needed for its intended operation.

Prelims focus

  • Hardware consists of physical computer components.
  • The motherboard connects major internal components.
  • The CPU executes instructions and performs processing.
  • RAM provides working memory; HDDs and SSDs provide persistent storage.
  • Peripheral devices support input, output, storage or related functions.
  • Trap: The desktop cabinet or system unit is not itself the CPU.

[Sources: IBM, What Is Computer Hardware?, sections on internal and external hardware and hardware components; CBSE, Installation Technician: Computing and Peripherals, Class XI, Chapter 2, Computer System Fundamentals; National Institute of Open Schooling, Data Entry Operations, Lesson 1, sections 1.3–1.6. Online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
